LAW:S02:DRC14:1b.text:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by any court or Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant:Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely: -
cite11†(b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

IK-190902:L107.text: 30. So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same. A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part. If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession: See Stenina v.

IK-190902:L108.text: Abrahama, (1931) f Ch D 470 and G. D. Chaudhary v. Anand Sarup. 1966 Delhi Lt 28.

IK-190902:L109.text: 31. Clause (b) of the proviso to cite8†Section 14(1) uses three expressions namely 'sublet', 'assign' and 'otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord'. These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

IK-190902:L110.text: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet. In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

IK-190902:L111.text: The expression "parted with possession" undoubtedly postulates parting with possession session means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession has been given by lease and "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.

IK-190902:L112.text: The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself or in other words there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession. The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession: See cite11†Hazari Lal v. Gian Ram . 1972 Ren Cr 74 (Delhi).

target_refs.quote: In the present case, it is not disputed that the premises had been let for residential purposes, but it is also beyond doubt that to the knowledge of the landlord the premises have been regularly used by the tenant not only for her own residence but also for her foreign guests.

original_proposal.reason: The Supreme Court expressly accepted that the premises had been let for residential purposes. The frozen input independently contains the statutory authorities' prior finding that the premises had been let for residential purposes, so the input contains sufficient support for this condition. The later failure of the section 14(1)(e) ground does not invert this condition.

target_refs.quote: Assuming that the bona fide requirement of the landlord is established, the landlord must still prove that the premises had been let for residential purposes.
Assuming that the bona fide requirement of the landlord is established, the landlord must still prove that the premises had been let for residential purposes.

original_proposal.reason: The Supreme Court expressly proceeded on an assumption that bona fide requirement was established rather than adjudicating that condition. The frozen input supplies no facts or prior finding concerning the landlord's bona fide residential requirement.

The Supreme Court did not substantively determine whether the claimed occupation was by the landlord herself or by a dependent family member. Its decisive reasoning concerned the residential-purpose characterization under the Explanation and the landlord's consent to the longstanding boarding-house use. The frozen input does not identify or support a qualifying occupation route.

target_refs.quote: The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964 and thus stepped into his shoes as the `landlord' as defined under section 2(e) of the Act.
The present respondent purchased the property from her father on 27th June, 1964 and thus stepped into his shoes as the `landlord' as defined under section 2(e) of the Act.

original_proposal.reason: The Supreme Court's accepted factual matrix states that the respondent purchased the property from the original landlord, supporting the ownership qualification. The frozen input, however, preserves only the respondent's relationship to the original landlord and the original letting; it omits the decisive purchase fact, so it is insufficient for this target.

The Supreme Court did not apply or determine the alternative route involving occupation by a person for whose benefit the premises were held. The frozen input contains no facts concerning such a person or such a holding arrangement.

The Supreme Court did not substantively determine whether the landlord or another qualifying person lacked other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. The reference near the end of the judgment to alternative accommodation concerns the separate case numbered 1870868, not this case, and the frozen input for case 1114159 supplies no accommodation evidence.

IK-1114159:L244:span5.text: The tenant contended that she had never parted with her exclusive possession of any part of the premises and the foreign students who were lodging were her paying guests and were not her tenants.

original_proposal.reason: The tenancy itself began on 19 May 1954, after 9 June 1952, and the Supreme Court accepted that sub-letting by that tenant was substantiated. The relevant sub-letting therefore necessarily occurred after the statutory cutoff. The frozen input contains the 1954 letting date and the prior section 14(1)(b) sub-letting finding, making the timing condition sufficiently supported.

target_refs.quote: Indisputably, sub-letting has been substantiated.
Arguments before us have proceeded on the footing that a sub-tenancy has been created and this amounts to a breach of condition with a provision for re-entry.

Arguments before us have proceeded on the footing that a sub-tenancy has been created and this amounts to a breach of condition with a provision for re-entry.

original_proposal.reason: The Supreme Court expressly treated sub-letting as substantiated and proceeded on the footing that a sub-tenancy had been created. That is a substantive acceptance of the subletting route rather than merely a procedural dismissal. The frozen input contains the Appellate Tribunal's prior finding upholding sub-letting under section 14(1)(b), which is sufficient to expose this legal route even though the detailed underlying proof of each tenancy incident is not separately reproduced.

The Supreme Court adjudicated the case on the footing of sub-letting/sub-tenancy and did not determine that the tenant assigned and divested himself of all tenant rights. The frozen input likewise contains no assignment allegation or finding.

The Supreme Court did not separately adjudicate the alternative parting-with-possession route or find that the tenant divested or abandoned his own right to possession. The case was treated as one of substantiated sub-letting, and the frozen input contains no possession-divestment facts.

This constitutes adoption of the no-consent component. The frozen input contains the same Tribunal finding of sub-letting without consent under section 14(1)(b), so it is sufficient for this condition.

The Supreme Court did not analyze that route or decide whether the tenant retained concurrent legal possession. The frozen input contains no facts addressing concurrent use or retention of possession.
